micros.title: Warm-up: Adding and Subtracting Integers
micros.description: Revise integer addition and subtraction with the number line and debt model, firmly separating them from the multiplication sign rules to come.
outcomes: Can add and subtract any two integers fluently
Can explain why (−3) + (−5) = −8 using the debt model

question.prompt: Compute: (−3) + (−5)

options.diagnosis: Subtracted the magnitudes (5 − 3) and kept a minus sign.
Subtracted the magnitudes and dropped the sign entirely.

question.explanation: Owing ₹3 and then owing ₹5 more means owing ₹8: (−3) + (−5) = −8. 'Minus and minus make plus' belongs to MULTIPLICATION, not addition — two debts never add up to a gain.

micros.title: Multiplying a Positive by a Negative
micros.description: Build 4 × (−3) as repeated addition of debts, and (−3) × 4 via commutativity, establishing that unlike signs give a negative product.
outcomes: Can compute products of one positive and one negative integer
Can justify the negative sign using repeated addition or a real context

micros.title: Why Negative × Negative Is Positive
micros.description: Use the descending pattern 3×(−6), 2×(−6), 1×(−6), 0×(−6), ... to force (−1)×(−6) = +6, and frame negative × negative as reversing a reversal.
outcomes: Can multiply two negative integers correctly
Can justify the sign of the product with the pattern argument

question.prompt: Compute: (−7) × (−3)

options.diagnosis: Added the magnitudes and kept a minus — treated × as +.
Added the magnitudes, then applied the sign rule — right rule, wrong operation.

question.explanation: Negative × negative = positive: (−7) × (−3) is the opposite of 7 × (−3) = −21, so it is +21. The pattern 3×(−3)=−9, 2×(−3)=−6, 1×(−3)=−3, 0×(−3)=0 keeps adding 3, so negative multipliers must continue into positives.

micros.title: Dividing Integers with Sign Rules
micros.description: Connect every division to its multiplication check — (−36) ÷ 4 = q means q × 4 = −36 — so the same sign rules govern quotients.
outcomes: Can divide integers with any combination of signs
Can verify a quotient's sign via the multiplication check

options.diagnosis: Subtracted 6 from 48 instead of dividing, and kept a minus.
Multiplied instead of dividing.

question.explanation: Check by multiplication: what times (−6) gives −48? Since 8 × (−6) = −48, the quotient is +8. Like signs (negative ÷ negative) always give a positive result — the same rule as multiplication.

micros.title: Properties of Operations and Opening Brackets
micros.description: Use commutativity, associativity and distributivity with negatives, reading −(a + b) as (−1) × (a + b) so the minus reaches EVERY term inside.
outcomes: Can use distributivity to simplify computations like (−4) × 103
Can expand −(a + b) correctly to −a − b and check numerically

question.prompt: Simplify: −(9 + 4)

options.diagnosis: Dropped the leading minus after adding.
Changed only the second term's sign, computing 9 − 4.

question.explanation: Read −(9 + 4) as (−1) × (9 + 4) and distribute to BOTH terms: −9 − 4 = −13. Check directly: the bracket is 13, and the opposite of 13 is −13 — so −5 (minus reaching only the 9) cannot be right.

micros.title: Multi-step Problems with All Four Operations
micros.description: Solve real contexts — quiz scoring, draining tanks, falling temperatures — that mix addition, subtraction, multiplication and division of integers.
outcomes: Can translate a signed real-world situation into an integer expression
Can evaluate multi-step integer expressions respecting order of operations

question.prompt: At 10 pm the temperature is 4°C and it falls 2°C every hour. What is the temperature 6 hours later?

options.diagnosis: Computed the total drop 6 × (−2) but forgot the starting 4°C.
Subtracted the 6 hours instead of the 12-degree total drop.

question.explanation: Final = 4 + 6 × (−2) = 4 − 12 = −8°C. Dropping the sign turns the fall into a rise and gives 4 + 12 = 16°C — a warm night instead of a freezing one.

micros.title: 'Of' Means Multiply: Fraction of a Quantity
micros.description: Interpret 3/4 of 20 as 3/4 × 20 with pictures and sharing, meeting the first surprise: taking a fraction OF something makes it smaller.
outcomes: Can find a fraction of a whole-number quantity
Can explain why multiplying by a fraction less than 1 shrinks the result

micros.title: Multiplying Fractions with the Area Model
micros.description: Multiply fractions 'tops times tops, bottoms times bottoms', backed by the shaded-rectangle area model so the rule has an image behind it.
outcomes: Can multiply two fractions and simplify the product
Can draw an area model showing why 2/3 × 4/5 = 8/15

question.prompt: Compute: 3/5 × 2/7

options.diagnosis: Added the fractions (21/35 + 10/35) instead of multiplying.
Added numerators and added denominators — a rule that fits neither operation.

question.explanation: Multiply straight across: (3 × 2)/(5 × 7) = 6/35. Cross-multiplying (3 × 7 over 5 × 2 = 21/10) belongs to comparing fractions, not multiplying — and 21/10 is bigger than 1, impossible for a product of two fractions below 1.

micros.title: Multiplying Mixed Numbers
micros.description: Convert mixed numbers to improper fractions before multiplying, and see with numbers why multiplying whole and fraction parts separately undercounts.
outcomes: Can multiply mixed numbers via improper fractions
Can estimate the product first to catch conversion errors

micros.title: Dividing by a Fraction: Keep–Change–Flip and Why
micros.description: Anchor a ÷ (1/2) in 'how many halves fit in a?', then formalise: keep the dividend, change ÷ to ×, flip the DIVISOR — and verify by multiplying back.
outcomes: Can divide fractions by inverting the divisor only
Can explain the reciprocal rule with a fitting-in picture and check answers by multiplication

question.prompt: Compute: 5/6 ÷ 2/3

options.diagnosis: Multiplied by 2/3 without flipping anything.
Inverted BOTH fractions before multiplying.

question.explanation: Keep–change–flip: 5/6 ÷ 2/3 = 5/6 × 3/2 = 15/12 = 5/4. Only the DIVISOR is inverted. Check: 5/4 × 2/3 = 10/12 = 5/6 ✓. Flipping the dividend instead gives 6/5 × 2/3 = 4/5, which fails the check.

micros.title: Multiplying Decimals: Counting Decimal Places
micros.description: Route decimal products through fractions (0.3 × 0.2 = 3/10 × 2/10 = 6/100), then formalise: the product carries as many decimal places as both factors combined.
outcomes: Can multiply decimals and place the point by counting places
Can catch place-value errors with an estimation check

question.prompt: Compute: 0.4 × 0.6

options.diagnosis: Multiplied 4 × 6 and ignored both decimal points.
Added the decimals instead of multiplying.

question.explanation: 4 × 6 = 24, and the factors have 1 + 1 = 2 decimal places between them, so the product has two: 0.24. Fraction check: 4/10 × 6/10 = 24/100. Sense check: 0.4 of 0.6 must be SMALLER than 0.6, ruling out 2.4.

micros.title: Dividing Decimals
micros.description: Divide decimals by whole numbers, then by decimals by scaling both numbers by the same power of 10 until the divisor is whole.
outcomes: Can divide a decimal by a whole number keeping the point aligned
Can divide by a decimal by shifting both points equally (3.6 ÷ 0.4 = 36 ÷ 4)

micros.title: Will the Answer Be Bigger or Smaller?
micros.description: Build the prediction habit: multiplying by a number less than 1 shrinks, dividing by a number less than 1 enlarges — overturning the primary-school instinct.
outcomes: Can predict whether a product or quotient exceeds the starting number before computing
Can state the boundary role of 1 in both operations

question.prompt: WITHOUT computing exactly, which expression has a value GREATER than 60?

options.diagnosis: Multiplying by a number below 1 shrinks: this is 45.
Dividing by a number above 1 shrinks: this is 50.

question.explanation: Dividing by 0.9 asks how many 0.9s fit in 60 — more than 60 of them (≈66.7). Multiplying by 0.9 takes nine-tenths OF 60, which is less (54). The instinct 'multiplication enlarges, division shrinks' only holds for numbers greater than 1.

micros.title: What Counts as a Rational Number
micros.description: Define rationals as p/q with integers p, q and q ≠ 0, and show integers and terminating decimals joining the family via 5 = 5/1 and 0.7 = 7/10.
outcomes: Can decide whether a given number is rational and write it as p/q
Can draw the nested-sets picture: integers inside rationals

question.prompt: Which statement about the number 5 is true?

options.text: It is a rational number, because 5 = 5/1
It is not rational, because it is not written as a fraction
It is an integer, so it cannot also be rational
It is rational only when written as 5.0
options.diagnosis: How a number is WRITTEN doesn't change what it is; 5, 5.0 and 5/1 are the same number.

question.explanation: A rational number is any number expressible as p/q with integers p, q and q ≠ 0. Since 5 = 5/1, it qualifies. Every integer is rational — the integers sit INSIDE the rational family, they are not excluded from it.

micros.title: Standard Form: Where the Sign Lives
micros.description: Establish that −5/8, 5/−8 and −(5/8) are one number, and write rationals in standard form: sign in the numerator, positive denominator, lowest terms.
outcomes: Can rewrite any rational with a positive denominator in lowest terms
Can recognise equivalent forms of the same negative rational

question.prompt: Write −8/−12 in standard form.

options.diagnosis: Left a negative denominator and stopped short of lowest terms.
Inverted the fraction while simplifying.

question.explanation: Two negative signs cancel: −8/−12 = 8/12. Divide top and bottom by the HCF 4: 2/3. The number is POSITIVE — a negative over a negative is like (−8) ÷ (−12), and like signs give a positive quotient.

micros.title: Rationals on the Number Line
micros.description: Place positive and negative rationals by subdividing the gaps between integers, locating numbers like −3/4 between −1 and 0.
outcomes: Can plot any rational number by subdividing unit intervals
Can read off the rational represented by a marked point

micros.title: Comparing and Ordering Rationals
micros.description: Compare rationals via common denominators and the number line, mastering the reflection principle: comparing negatives reverses the comparison of their positives.
outcomes: Can order a mixed list of positive and negative rationals
Can explain why −3/4 < −1/2 although 3/4 > 1/2

question.prompt: Which number is SMALLER: −2/3 or −1/3?

options.diagnosis: Different numerators over the same denominator are different numbers.
Every pair of rationals can be compared — the number line orders them all.

question.explanation: On the number line −2/3 sits further LEFT than −1/3, so it is smaller. For negatives, bigger magnitude means a smaller number — the comparison of 2/3 > 1/3 gets REVERSED by the minus signs.

micros.title: Finding Rationals Between Rationals
micros.description: Use averaging and denominator enlargement (1/3 = 10/30, 1/2 = 15/30) to exhibit rationals between any two given ones — and see the supply never ends.
outcomes: Can find several rationals between two given rationals
Can argue that infinitely many rationals lie between any two distinct rationals

question.prompt: How many rational numbers lie between 1/4 and 1/2?

options.text: None — they are next to each other
Only the ones with denominator up to 8
options.diagnosis: Denominators can be as large as you like — 9/32, 100/399, ... keep appearing forever.

question.explanation: The average 3/8 lies between them; then the average of 1/4 and 3/8 lies between THOSE; and so on without end. Rewriting as 8/32 and 16/32 already shows seven thirty-secondths strictly between — and finer denominators reveal ever more.

micros.title: Fractions, Decimals and Percents: One Family
micros.description: Convert fluently between the three notations — 3/5 = 0.6 = 60% — reading percent as 'per hundred' throughout.
outcomes: Can convert any of fraction, decimal, percent into the other two
Can recall benchmark equivalents (1/2, 1/4, 3/4, 1/5, 1/10)

micros.title: Finding a Percent of a Quantity
micros.description: Compute p% of a quantity by translating the percent into a fraction EVERY time: 15% of 400 = 15/100 × 400 — the rate must act on the base.
outcomes: Can find a given percent of a quantity
Can keep the rate (%) and the result (units) clearly separate

question.prompt: Find 15% of 400.

options.diagnosis: Subtracted 15 from 400 — treated the percent as an amount to remove.

question.explanation: 15% = 15/100, so 15% of 400 = (15 × 400)/100 = 60. Answering '15' repeats the rate without applying it; 6000 comes from 15 × 400 with the /100 dropped — off by exactly a factor of 100.

micros.title: Expressing One Quantity as a Percent of Another
micros.description: Turn part/whole comparisons into percents to compare unlike bases fairly — 18 out of 25 versus 68 out of 100 — always asking 'percent OF WHAT?'.
outcomes: Can express one quantity as a percentage of another
Can compare quantities with different bases by converting both to percents

question.prompt: Ria scored 18 out of 25 in one test; Sam scored 68 out of 100 in another. Who did better?

options.text: Sam — 68 marks is more than 18 marks

options.diagnosis: 72% ≠ 68%; equal raw gaps do not mean equal shares of different totals.

options.text: Scores from different tests can never be compared
options.diagnosis: That is exactly what percentages are FOR — converting to the common base 100.

question.explanation: Convert both to the base 100: 18/25 = 72/100 = 72%, while Sam has 68%. Comparing the raw marks 68 vs 18 ignores that the totals differ — percent-of-different-bases must be converted before comparing.

micros.title: Percentage Increase and Decrease
micros.description: Compute percent change on the ORIGINAL value, and discover with ₹100 → ₹110 → ₹99 why an x% rise followed by an x% cut does not return home.
outcomes: Can compute percentage increase or decrease of a quantity
Can explain why successive +10% and −10% changes do not cancel

question.prompt: A price of ₹200 is raised by 10%, and the new price is then reduced by 10%. What is the final price?

options.diagnosis: Applied only the increase and stopped.
Took both 10% amounts from the ORIGINAL ₹200; the cut acts on ₹220.

question.explanation: ₹200 + 10% = ₹220; then ₹220 − 10% of 220 = 220 − 22 = ₹198. The rise and cut use DIFFERENT bases (200, then 220), so they cannot cancel — you end ₹2 below the start.

micros.title: Profit and Loss Percent on the Cost Price
micros.description: Compute profit or loss in rupees and as a percent whose base is always the COST price — the money originally invested.
outcomes: Can compute profit/loss and profit/loss percent from CP and SP
Can find SP given CP and a profit percent (and vice versa in simple cases)

question.prompt: A shopkeeper buys a lamp for ₹250 (CP) and sells it for ₹300 (SP). What is the profit percent?

options.diagnosis: Reported the rupee profit (₹50) with a percent sign attached.
Computed SP as a percent of CP but forgot to subtract the original 100%.

question.explanation: Profit = 300 − 250 = ₹50. Profit% = 50/250 × 100 = 20%. Dividing by the selling price (50/300 ≈ 16.7%) uses the wrong base — profit percent measures how much the money INVESTED grew, so the base is CP.

micros.title: Simple Interest and the Amount
micros.description: Use SI = P × R × T / 100 for deposits and loans, keeping interest and the final amount (principal + interest) clearly distinct.
outcomes: Can compute simple interest given principal, rate and time
Can find the amount and solve for one missing quantity in the formula

micros.title: Reading and Writing Powers
micros.description: Read a^n as 'a used as a factor n times', evaluating small powers and contrasting 2³ = 8 with 2 × 3 = 6 until the two never blur.
outcomes: Can evaluate powers with whole-number bases and exponents
Can express a repeated product in exponential form and identify base and exponent

question.prompt: What is 3⁴?

options.diagnosis: Swapped base and exponent: computed 4³.
Added base and exponent.

question.explanation: 3⁴ means 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 81 — the base 3 used as a factor four times. It is NOT 3 × 4 = 12; compare 10² = 100 with 10 × 2 = 20 to feel how different the two are.

micros.title: Powers of Negative Bases
micros.description: Track the sign of (−a)^n through the sign rules: even exponents give positive results, odd exponents keep the minus — and (−2)⁴ differs from −2⁴.
outcomes: Can evaluate powers of negative integers
Can predict the sign of (−a)^n from the parity of n

micros.title: Product Law: Add the Exponents
micros.description: Derive a^m × a^n = a^(m+n) by expanding both powers into factors at least once, so the shortcut is earned rather than memorised.
outcomes: Can simplify products of same-base powers by adding exponents
Can justify the law by expansion and spot when it does NOT apply (different bases)

question.prompt: Simplify: 5³ × 5⁴

options.diagnosis: Multiplied the bases as well; with the same base, the base stays put.

question.explanation: 5³ × 5⁴ = (5·5·5) × (5·5·5·5) = seven 5s multiplied = 5⁷. Multiplying same-base powers ADDS the exponents (3 + 4 = 7); multiplying them (3 × 4 = 12) counts factors that are not there.

micros.title: Quotient Law and Why a⁰ = 1
micros.description: Derive a^m ÷ a^n = a^(m−n) by cancelling factors, then walk the ladder 7³, 7², 7¹, 7⁰ — each step divides by 7 — to land on a⁰ = 1.
outcomes: Can simplify quotients of same-base powers by subtracting exponents
Can explain via the ladder or quotient law why a⁰ = 1 for a ≠ 0

question.prompt: What is 9⁰?

options.diagnosis: Glued the digits together — the exponent is not a digit to append.

question.explanation: Walk down: 9² = 81, 9¹ = 9, and each step divides by 9 — so 9⁰ = 9/9 = 1. Or use the quotient law: 9² ÷ 9² = 9⁰, and any number divided by itself is 1.

micros.title: Power of a Power and Power of a Product
micros.description: Establish (a^m)^n = a^(mn) and (ab)^m = a^m b^m by expansion, completing the toolkit of exponent laws.
outcomes: Can simplify expressions like (2³)² and (3 × 5)²
Can choose the correct law when several could apply

micros.title: Standard Form for Large Numbers
micros.description: Write large numbers as k × 10^n with 1 ≤ k < 10, choosing the power by counting DECIMAL SHIFTS from after the leading digit — not by counting zeros.
outcomes: Can express large numbers in standard form and convert back
Can compare magnitudes of numbers given in standard form

question.prompt: Write 5,600,000 in standard form.

options.diagnosis: Equal in value, but standard form needs the first factor at least 1 and less than 10.
Off by one: counted all seven digits instead of the six decimal shifts.

question.explanation: Place the point after the leading digit: 5.6. The point must move 6 places to restore 5,600,000, so the power is 10⁶. Counting only the five zeros undercounts — the 6 after the 5 also gets crossed by the moving point.

micros.title: What an Equation Says
micros.description: Read '=' as 'both sides weigh the same' — a statement, not an instruction to compute — using equations written in every orientation, including 12 = x + 5.
outcomes: Can state what an equation claims and identify its two sides
Can decide whether a given value makes an equation true or false

question.prompt: What does the equation 12 = x + 5 tell us?

options.text: That x + 5 and 12 are the same value — so x must be 7
That x is 12, since 12 is the answer written first
That the equation is written backwards and has no solution

options.diagnosis: Added 5 to 12 instead of asking what plus 5 gives 12.

question.explanation: '=' declares that the two sides balance; it does not announce a result. 12 = x + 5 and x + 5 = 12 say exactly the same thing, and the value keeping the balance is x = 7 (since 7 + 5 = 12).

micros.title: The Balance Model: Same Move on Both Sides
micros.description: Use a pan balance (drawn or physical) to see that adding, subtracting, multiplying or dividing must hit BOTH sides, or the equation tips into falsehood.
outcomes: Can perform the same operation on both sides and keep the equation true
Can spot and explain the error when an operation touches only one side

question.prompt: To solve x/4 = 3, which move is correct?

options.text: Multiply BOTH sides by 4, giving x = 12
Multiply only the left side by 4, giving x = 3
Divide both sides by 4, giving x = 3/4
options.diagnosis: Chose the SAME operation instead of the inverse — dividing again buries x deeper.

options.text: Subtract 4 from both sides, giving x = −1
options.diagnosis: Treated the ÷4 as a +4; the inverse of dividing is multiplying.

question.explanation: x is divided by 4, so undo it by multiplying — but on BOTH sides: x/4 × 4 = 3 × 4 gives x = 12. Check: 12/4 = 3 ✓. Multiplying one side only changes what the equation says and breaks the balance.

micros.title: Solving by Inverse Operations
micros.description: Solve one- and two-step equations like 3x + 4 = 19 by peeling operations off in reverse order, deriving 'transposition' honestly from both-sides moves.
outcomes: Can solve two-step linear equations including negative solutions
Can narrate each transposition as its underlying both-sides operation

question.prompt: Solve: 3x + 4 = 19

options.diagnosis: Reached 3x = 15 but then multiplied by 3 instead of dividing.
Stopped at 3x = 15 and reported it as x.

question.explanation: Subtract 4 from both sides: 3x = 15. Divide both sides by 3: x = 5. Check: 3(5) + 4 = 19 ✓. Moving the +4 across WITHOUT flipping it to −4 gives 3x = 23 and the wrong x = 23/3 — the check exposes it.

micros.title: Check Your Solution by Substitution
micros.description: Make substitution the mandatory last step of every solve: put the value back into the ORIGINAL equation and record a ✓ or ✗ — a failed check locates the wrong move.
outcomes: Can verify a proposed solution by substituting into the original equation
Can use a failed check to hunt down the erroneous step

question.prompt: A student claims x = 4 solves 5x − 3 = 12. Is the claim right?

options.text: No — substituting gives 5(4) − 3 = 17 ≠ 12; the real solution is x = 3
Yes — the working looked correct, so there is no need to check
No — because 5(4) = 9, so the left side is 6
options.diagnosis: Added 5 and 4 instead of multiplying; the check itself must be computed correctly.

options.text: It cannot be judged without re-solving the whole equation
options.diagnosis: Substitution alone settles it — that is the power of checking.

question.explanation: Substitute: 5(4) − 3 = 20 − 3 = 17, not 12, so x = 4 fails. Solving properly: 5x = 15, x = 3, and 5(3) − 3 = 12 ✓. A ten-second substitution catches errors that neat-looking working hides.

micros.title: First Steps with the Variable on Both Sides
micros.description: Solve equations like 5x = 2x + 9 by collecting the variable terms on one side with balance moves — a gentle preview of the Class 8 staple.
outcomes: Can solve simple equations with the variable appearing on both sides
Can decide which side to collect variable terms on and why

micros.title: From Words to Equations
micros.description: Translate word problems — fares, recharges, consecutive numbers — into equations: name the unknown, encode the relationships, solve, and answer the question actually asked.
outcomes: Can set up a linear equation from a word problem
Can solve it and interpret the solution back in context

question.prompt: When 7 is added to twice a number, the result is 25. What is the number?

options.diagnosis: Stopped at 2x = 18 without dividing by 2.
Divided 25 by 2 before subtracting the 7 — inverse operations applied in the wrong order.

question.explanation: The equation is 2x + 7 = 25. Subtract 7: 2x = 18; divide by 2: x = 9. Check: 2(9) + 7 = 25 ✓. Transposing +7 without flipping gives 2x = 32 and x = 16 — but 2(16) + 7 = 39, so the check rejects it.

micros.title: Terms, Factors and Coefficients
micros.description: Take expressions apart with tree diagrams: terms are joined by + and −, each term is a product of factors, and the numerical factor is the coefficient — including the invisible 1 in x and −1 in −x.
outcomes: Can list the terms and factors of an expression
Can state the coefficient of any term, including lone and negated variables

question.prompt: What is the coefficient of x in the expression x + 5?

options.diagnosis: Picked the constant term; the coefficient multiplies the variable.

question.explanation: x means 1·x, so its coefficient is 1 — invisible but present. Writing the hidden 1 (and the hidden −1 in −x) explicitly is what makes combining like terms reliable later.

micros.title: Monomials, Binomials, Trinomials
micros.description: Classify expressions by their number of (unlike) terms, first simplifying so that disguised like terms don't inflate the count.
outcomes: Can classify expressions as monomial, binomial or trinomial
Can explain why 3x + 2x is a monomial in disguise

micros.title: Like Terms and How to Combine Them
micros.description: Sort terms into bins by their EXACT variable part and add coefficients within a bin — verifying with number substitution that unlike terms refuse to merge.
outcomes: Can identify like terms among terms with several variables and powers
Can combine like terms and leave unlike terms alone

question.prompt: Simplify: 4x + 3y

options.diagnosis: Added the coefficients and dropped the y — the terms have different variables.
Multiplied the coefficients as well as gluing the variables.

question.explanation: 4x and 3y are UNLIKE terms — different variable parts — so they cannot merge. Test with x = 2, y = 3: 4x + 3y = 17 but 7xy = 42. Like '4 samosas + 3 teas', the sum stays as two separate counts.

micros.title: Adding Algebraic Expressions
micros.description: Add whole expressions by regrouping like terms, horizontally and in columns, keeping every sign attached to its term.
outcomes: Can add two or three expressions and simplify the result
Can verify an addition by substituting a test value

micros.title: Subtracting Expressions: The Minus Reaches Every Term
micros.description: Rewrite subtraction as adding (−1) × (bracket) and distribute the −1 to EVERY term with drawn arrows, then combine like terms.
outcomes: Can subtract one expression from another, flipping every sign in the subtrahend
Can check the result numerically

question.prompt: Simplify: (5x + 2y) − (3x − 4y)

options.diagnosis: Subtracted the first expression from the second — order reversed.
Added the two brackets instead of subtracting.

question.explanation: Distribute the minus over BOTH terms of the second bracket: 5x + 2y − 3x + 4y. Combine: (5x − 3x) + (2y + 4y) = 2x + 6y. Leaving −4y unflipped gives 2x − 2y — the classic first-term-only slip.

micros.title: Evaluating Expressions, Including Negative Values
micros.description: Substitute values with bracket discipline — always (−2)², never bare −2² — and evaluate expressions used in perimeter and pattern formulas.
outcomes: Can evaluate an expression at given positive and negative values
Can distinguish (−2)² from −(2²) and compute each correctly

question.prompt: Evaluate x² − 3x when x = −2.

options.diagnosis: Computed −3 × (−2) as −6 instead of +6 — a sign slip in the second term.

question.explanation: Substitute with brackets: (−2)² − 3(−2) = 4 + 6 = 10. The trap is (−2)² = +4: squaring a negative gives a positive. Treating it as −4 yields 2 (or −10 with a second slip) — bracket discipline prevents both.

micros.title: Complementary and Supplementary Angles
micros.description: Find partners to 90° (Corner) and 180° (Straight), anchoring which word goes with which number so the two never swap.
outcomes: Can compute the complement and supplement of a given angle
Can classify a pair of angles as complementary, supplementary or neither

question.prompt: What is the supplement of 60°?

options.diagnosis: Subtracted from 360° — a full turn, not a straight line.
Thought 'supplement' means an equal partner angle.

question.explanation: Supplementary angles sum to 180° (Straight line): 180 − 60 = 120°. The 30° answer is the COMPLEMENT (to 90°, a Corner) — C before S, just as 90 comes before 180.

micros.title: Adjacent Angles and Linear Pairs
micros.description: Identify adjacent angles (common arm, common vertex, no overlap) and see that a linear pair — adjacent angles on a straight line — always totals 180°.
outcomes: Can identify adjacent angles and linear pairs in a figure
Can find the missing angle of a linear pair

micros.title: Vertically Opposite Angles Are Equal
micros.description: At any crossing of two lines, rotate a traced copy 180° to see opposite angles coincide — EQUAL, while the adjacent pairs are the ones summing to 180°.
outcomes: Can find all four angles at a crossing from any one of them
Can justify why vertically opposite angles are equal using linear pairs

question.prompt: Two lines intersect and one of the angles formed is 40°. What is the angle vertically opposite to it?

options.diagnosis: Subtracted from 360° — the four angles together make 360°, but the opposite one alone doesn't.

question.explanation: Vertically opposite angles are always EQUAL: 40°. The two angles ADJACENT to it are its supplements, 140° each — that is where the 140° answer belongs. (And 50° is the complement, a 90° idea that has no role at a plain crossing.)

micros.title: Naming Angle Pairs at a Transversal
micros.description: When a transversal cuts two lines, learn to NAME the eight angles' relationships — corresponding (F), alternate (Z), co-interior (C/U) — before any equality rules are invoked.
outcomes: Can identify corresponding, alternate interior/exterior and co-interior pairs
Can locate a named pair in any orientation of the figure

micros.title: Angle Rules for Parallel Lines
micros.description: With parallel lines, corresponding and alternate angles are EQUAL while co-interior angles are SUPPLEMENTARY — sorted physically with tracing-paper slides and half-turns.
outcomes: Can compute every angle at a transversal of parallel lines from one given angle
Can justify each step by naming the pair and its rule

question.prompt: A transversal cuts two parallel lines. One of a pair of CO-INTERIOR angles is 40°. What is the other?

options.diagnosis: Subtracted from 360°; co-interior angles complete a straight 180°, not a full turn.

question.explanation: Co-interior (allied) angles between parallel lines are SUPPLEMENTARY: 180 − 40 = 140°. It is the corresponding and alternate pairs that are equal — the co-interior pair instead forms the 'C/U' shape summing to 180°.

micros.title: Are These Lines Parallel? Rules Need a Licence
micros.description: Use the converses — equal corresponding/alternate angles, or supplementary co-interior angles, certify parallelism — and never apply parallel-line rules without first stating which lines are parallel and why.
outcomes: Can test whether two lines are parallel from measured transversal angles
Can reject a rule application when the parallel condition is unverified

question.prompt: A transversal makes alternate angles of 60° and 70° with lines l and m. What can you conclude?

options.text: l and m are NOT parallel — alternate angles of parallel lines would be equal
l and m are parallel, because alternate angles are always equal
l and m are parallel, because 60 + 70 is less than 180
options.diagnosis: Garbled test: co-interior angles must sum to EXACTLY 180°, and these aren't co-interior anyway.

options.text: Nothing can be concluded from just two angles
options.diagnosis: Unequal alternate angles DO settle it — the equality test fails, so the lines are not parallel.

question.explanation: The rule 'alternate angles are equal' holds ONLY for parallel lines — it is a property with a licence condition. Since 60° ≠ 70°, the licence is refused: these lines must meet somewhere. The rules never apply to arbitrary crossing lines.

micros.title: Medians and Altitudes of a Triangle
micros.description: Meet the triangle's internal lines: a median joins a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side; an altitude drops perpendicularly from a vertex — sometimes landing outside the triangle.
outcomes: Can draw the three medians and three altitudes of a triangle
Can explain when an altitude falls outside the triangle

micros.title: The Angle Sum Is 180°
micros.description: Tear the corners off paper triangles and line them up along a ruler edge — a straight 180°, never a full turn — then compute unknown angles with the property.
outcomes: Can find the third angle of a triangle from the other two
Can solve angle problems combining the angle sum with linear pairs

question.prompt: Two angles of a triangle are 55° and 65°. What is the third angle?

options.diagnosis: Added the two given angles but never subtracted from 180°.
Assumed the triangle must be right-angled — nothing in the data says so.

question.explanation: Angles of a triangle sum to 180°: 180 − (55 + 65) = 60°. Using 360° gives the impossible 240° — 360° belongs to quadrilaterals and full turns, not triangles.

micros.title: The Exterior Angle Property
micros.description: Extend one side and colour-code the two REMOTE interior angles: the exterior angle equals their sum, provable two ways via the angle sum and the straight line.
outcomes: Can compute an exterior angle from the two remote interior angles
Can find a remote interior angle given the exterior angle

question.prompt: In a triangle, the two interior angles remote from an exterior angle measure 35° and 45°. What is the exterior angle?

options.diagnosis: Subtracted the remote angles instead of adding them.
Subtracted only 35° from 180° — used one remote angle as if it were the adjacent one.

question.explanation: Exterior angle = sum of the two REMOTE interior angles = 35 + 45 = 80°. The angle of 100° is the ADJACENT interior angle (180 − 80) — the neighbour on the straight line, not the exterior angle's value.

micros.title: Isosceles and Equilateral Triangle Angles
micros.description: Use 'angles opposite equal sides are equal' to solve isosceles and equilateral angle problems, combining it with the angle-sum property.
outcomes: Can find base angles of an isosceles triangle from the apex angle and vice versa
Can justify why every equilateral triangle has three 60° angles

micros.title: The Triangle Inequality
micros.description: Fail to close a triangle with sticks of lengths 3, 4 and 8, then formulate the rule from the experience: each side must be less than the sum of the other two.
outcomes: Can test whether three lengths can form a triangle
Can find the possible range for a third side given two sides

question.prompt: Can the lengths 5 cm, 6 cm and 12 cm form a triangle?

options.text: No — 5 + 6 = 11 < 12, so the two shorter sides cannot reach across the longest
Yes — any three lengths can form a triangle

options.diagnosis: Garbled test: compare the sum of TWO sides with the third, not the total with one side.

options.text: No — because a triangle's sides must all be within 3 cm of each other
options.diagnosis: Invented rule; the real test is the triangle inequality.

question.explanation: Each side must be shorter than the sum of the other two. Here 5 + 6 = 11 < 12, so the sides cannot close — sticks of these lengths physically fail to make a triangle.

micros.title: The Pythagoras Property of Right Triangles
micros.description: In RIGHT triangles only, the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the legs — used to find missing sides and to test for right angles.
outcomes: Can find a missing side of a right triangle in simple whole-number cases
Can use the converse to check whether a triangle is right-angled

question.prompt: A triangle has sides 5, 12 and 13. Is it right-angled?

options.text: Yes — 5² + 12² = 25 + 144 = 169 = 13², so the angle opposite the 13-side is right
Every triangle satisfies a² + b² = c², so the check proves nothing
No — Pythagoras only relates lengths and can say nothing about angles
options.diagnosis: The CONVERSE of Pythagoras is exactly an angle test: if the squares balance, the angle is right.

options.text: It cannot be decided without measuring an angle with a protractor
options.diagnosis: The numerical check settles it — that is the power of the converse.

question.explanation: Since 5² + 12² = 169 = 13², the converse of the Pythagoras property guarantees a right angle opposite the longest side. The relation is special to right triangles — acute and obtuse triangles fail it in opposite directions.

micros.title: What Congruence Means
micros.description: Two figures are congruent when one superposes exactly on the other — same shape AND size — which is stronger than merely having equal areas or looking alike.
outcomes: Can decide congruence of simple figures by superposition reasoning
Can give examples of equal-area figures that are not congruent

question.prompt: A 2 cm × 6 cm rectangle and a 3 cm × 4 cm rectangle both have area 12 cm². Are they congruent?

options.text: No — laid on top of each other they do not coincide
Yes — equal areas make figures congruent
Yes — both are rectangles, so they have the same shape
options.diagnosis: 'Rectangle' is a family, not a single shape; their proportions differ.

options.text: No — two rectangles can never be congruent to each other
options.diagnosis: Over-correction: two rectangles with the SAME length and breadth are congruent.

question.explanation: Congruence demands exact superposition — every side and angle matching. The 2×6 and 3×4 rectangles share an area but no placement makes them coincide. Equal area is necessary for congruence, never sufficient.

micros.title: Correspondence and Reading Off Equal Parts
micros.description: In ΔABC ≅ ΔPQR the letter positions ARE the matching: A↔P, B↔Q, C↔R. Read all six equal parts from the statement alone — that is CPCT.
outcomes: Can write a congruence statement in the correct vertex order
Can extract all corresponding equal sides and angles from a stated congruence

question.prompt: Given ΔPQR ≅ ΔXYZ, which side must be equal to PQ?

options.text: It cannot be determined from the statement
options.diagnosis: The letter order IS the correspondence — it fully determines every matching part.

question.explanation: Vertices correspond by position: P↔X, Q↔Y, R↔Z. So side PQ (1st–2nd letters) matches side XY (1st–2nd letters). Reading pairs by position is exactly what 'corresponding parts of congruent triangles' means.

micros.title: The SSS Criterion
micros.description: Three matched sides force congruence: a triangle with fixed side lengths is rigid — the reason trusses and brackets are triangular.
outcomes: Can apply SSS to justify congruence of two triangles
Can connect SSS to the rigidity of triangles in structures

micros.title: SAS: The Angle Must Be Included
micros.description: Two sides with the angle BETWEEN them determine a triangle; the same data with a non-included angle (SSA) can produce two different triangles.
outcomes: Can apply SAS with the included angle correctly identified
Can reject an SAS claim when the given angle is not between the given sides

question.prompt: In ΔABC and ΔDEF we know AB = DE, BC = EF and ∠A = ∠D. Can we conclude congruence by SAS?

options.text: No — the equal angle must lie BETWEEN the equal sides, which here would be ∠B and ∠E
Yes — two sides and any equal angle is exactly what SAS needs

options.diagnosis: ASA needs TWO angles with the included side; only one angle pair is known here.

options.text: No — congruence always requires all six parts to be checked
options.diagnosis: Three well-chosen parts suffice; the issue here is the arrangement, not the count.

question.explanation: ∠A is not between AB and BC — the included angle for those sides is ∠B. With a non-included angle (SSA) the compass arc can cross the ray twice, giving two different triangles, so no conclusion follows.

micros.title: ASA and RHS Criteria
micros.description: Two angles with the included side (ASA) pin a triangle down; for right triangles, the hypotenuse and one side (RHS) suffice — completing the toolkit of four criteria.
outcomes: Can apply ASA and RHS to justify congruence
Can select the appropriate criterion from the data given

micros.title: Why AAA and SSA Fail
micros.description: Nested equilateral triangles kill AAA (same angles, different sizes); the double-crossing compass arc kills SSA — sharpening what a criterion must guarantee.
outcomes: Can produce a counterexample showing AAA does not force congruence
Can explain the ambiguous case that defeats SSA

question.prompt: Two triangles have all three pairs of corresponding angles equal. Must they be congruent?

options.text: Not necessarily — one may be an enlargement of the other
Yes, as long as they are drawn the same way up
No — equal angles tell us nothing about the triangles
options.diagnosis: Over-correction: equal angles DO fix the shape (similarity); they just leave the size free.

question.explanation: Equal angles make triangles SIMILAR, not necessarily congruent: a small and a large equilateral triangle share all angles. Fixing the size needs at least one side — which is why every genuine criterion contains an S.

micros.title: Line Symmetry Revisited — Fold Tests, Not Guesses
micros.description: Re-establish mirror lines by folding, including the surprise that a generic parallelogram has NONE — its diagonal fold leaves flipped, non-matching halves.
outcomes: Can count the lines of symmetry of standard polygons by fold reasoning
Can explain why a parallelogram's diagonals are not mirror lines

question.prompt: How many lines of symmetry does a generic parallelogram (not a rectangle or rhombus) have?

options.text: 1 — a vertical line through the middle
options.diagnosis: That fold matches a rectangle, not a slanted parallelogram.
Copied the square's count; the parallelogram loses every one of those folds.

question.explanation: Fold a paper parallelogram along a diagonal: the two halves are congruent but flipped the wrong way, so they do NOT coincide. No fold works at all — the parallelogram's symmetry is rotational (a half-turn), not mirror.

micros.title: Rotational Symmetry and Its Order
micros.description: Rotate a marked cut-out through a full turn and tally every position where the outline matches — the order counts ALL matches in 360°, including the return home.
outcomes: Can find the order of rotational symmetry of a figure by rotation-tallying
Can explain why every figure has order at least 1

question.prompt: What is the order of rotational symmetry of an equilateral triangle?

options.diagnosis: Added the 3 mirror lines to the 3 rotations — mixing the two kinds of symmetry.

question.explanation: Rotating about the centre, the outline matches at 120°, 240° and 360° — three positions in one full turn, so order 3. The 120° is the ANGLE of rotation; the order is the COUNT of matches, including the final return.

micros.title: Angle of Rotation and the Centre
micros.description: Pin down angle = 360° ÷ order with a table (order 2 ↔ 180°, order 3 ↔ 120°, order 4 ↔ 90°) and locate the centre of rotation of symmetric figures.
outcomes: Can compute the smallest angle of rotation from the order and vice versa
Can locate the centre of rotation of a figure

micros.title: Line and Rotational Symmetry Are Independent
micros.description: Fill a 2×2 sorting grid with counterexamples in every cell — square (both), isosceles trapezium (line only), parallelogram and letter S (rotation only), scalene triangle (neither).
outcomes: Can give an example shape for each combination of line/rotational symmetry
Can classify a given figure into the correct cell of the grid

question.prompt: Which shape has rotational symmetry but NO line of symmetry?

options.text: No such shape can exist — the two symmetries always come together

options.diagnosis: A square has BOTH: four mirror lines and rotational order 4.
The opposite cell: one mirror line but only trivial rotational symmetry (order 1).

question.explanation: A half-turn about the diagonals' intersection maps a parallelogram onto itself (order 2), yet no fold ever works. The letter S is another such shape. Line and rotational symmetry are independent properties — every combination occurs.

micros.title: Faces, Edges and Vertices
micros.description: Attach each word to a gesture on a real solid — palm on a FACE, finger along an EDGE, fingertip on a VERTEX — and tabulate F, E, V for cubes, cuboids, prisms and pyramids.
outcomes: Can count faces, edges and vertices of common solids
Can keep the three words attached to the right parts, counting hidden ones from a sketch

question.prompt: How many edges does a cube have?
question.explanation: A cube has 12 edges — 4 around the top, 4 around the bottom, 4 vertical. The counts 6 and 8 belong to its faces and vertices; and 9 is what you get counting only the edges VISIBLE in a sketch, forgetting the hidden three.

micros.title: Nets That Fold — and Nets That Don't
micros.description: Fold printed 6-square arrangements to discover which become cubes, building checking strategies (no 2×2 block, at most four in a row) from real failures; extend to cuboid, cylinder and cone nets.
outcomes: Can decide whether a given net folds into a given solid
Can draw at least two distinct valid nets of a cube

question.prompt: Which of these arrangements of six squares folds into a cube?

options.text: A cross: four squares in a column with one square attached on each side of the second square
A 2 × 3 rectangular block of six squares
A straight strip of six squares in a row
A plus sign made of five squares
options.diagnosis: A cube has six faces; five squares can never close it.

question.explanation: The cross folds up cleanly: the four column squares wrap around, the two side squares cap the ends. The 2×3 block and the straight strip both overlap some faces and leave others open — having six squares is necessary but far from sufficient.

micros.title: Oblique and Isometric Sketches
micros.description: Draw solids two ways — oblique sketches on plain paper and isometric sketches on dot paper — marking hidden edges dashed and keeping a real cube in hand while drawing.
outcomes: Can make an oblique sketch of a cube or cuboid with hidden edges dashed
Can draw a cuboid of given dimensions on isometric dot paper

micros.title: Cross-sections: The Cut's Direction Decides
micros.description: Slice solids (clay, cucumber) horizontally AND vertically and trace the exposed faces — a cylinder yields a circle one way and a rectangle the other; the direction of cut is part of every answer.
outcomes: Can name the cross-section from a described horizontal or vertical cut
Can explain why one solid can produce different cross-sections

question.prompt: A cone is cut VERTICALLY, straight down through its apex. What is the shape of the cut face?

options.diagnosis: That comes from a SLANTED cut, not a vertical one through the apex.
A vertical cut gives a rectangle for a CYLINDER; the cone tapers to its apex.

question.explanation: Cutting through the apex and straight down exposes a triangle — the two slant sides meet at the tip. Circles come only from HORIZONTAL cuts of the cone. The cross-section's shape depends on the cut's direction, not just the solid.

micros.title: Top, Front and Side Views; Shadows
micros.description: Read and draw the three standard views of cube arrangements and everyday objects, and reason about the shadows solids cast — different 2D pictures of one 3D reality.
outcomes: Can draw top, front and side views of a simple solid arrangement
Can match a solid to its set of three views

micros.title: Constructing a Parallel Line Through a Point
micros.description: Draw a transversal through the external point, then copy its angle with compass arcs at the new point — equal alternate/corresponding angles GUARANTEE parallelism, no eyeballing.
outcomes: Can construct a line through a given point parallel to a given line
Can justify the construction via the equal-angles condition for parallel lines

question.prompt: Why does copying the transversal's angle at point P produce a line through P parallel to l?

options.text: Because equal corresponding (or alternate) angles are exactly the condition that makes two lines parallel
Because sliding the ruler carefully keeps the new line looking parallel
Because the compass keeps the same radius, so the lines stay the same distance apart
options.diagnosis: Equal arc radii copy an ANGLE; the constant-distance property is a consequence, not the mechanism.

options.text: Because any line through P that misses l on the page is parallel to it
options.diagnosis: Lines extend beyond the page — not meeting in the drawing is not the same as never meeting.

question.explanation: The construction builds the parallel CONDITION directly into the figure: the copied angle forces equal corresponding/alternate angles with the transversal, and lines making equal such angles can never meet. That is why no visual judgement is needed.

micros.title: Constructing a Triangle from Three Sides (SSS)
micros.description: Lay the base, then swing arcs of the other two lengths from its ends — after FIRST checking the triangle inequality, so doomed data is caught before the compass moves.
outcomes: Can construct a triangle from three given side lengths
Can predict from the triangle inequality when the arcs will fail to meet

question.prompt: You try to construct a triangle with sides 6 cm, 7 cm and 14 cm. What happens?

options.text: It is impossible — the arcs of radius 6 and 7 can never meet, since 6 + 7 < 14
It works if you draw bigger, more careful arcs
It works — any three lengths give a triangle
It is impossible because two of the sides ought to be equal
options.diagnosis: Scalene triangles are perfectly constructible; the real obstacle is the triangle inequality.

question.explanation: From the ends of the 14 cm base, arcs of radii 6 and 7 reach a combined 13 cm at full stretch — they can never intersect. No compass technique fixes data that violates the triangle inequality; check it BEFORE constructing.

micros.title: Constructing a Triangle from SAS
micros.description: Draw one side, copy the given angle AT ITS END, and mark the second side along the new ray — the angle must sit BETWEEN the two given sides for the triangle to be unique.
outcomes: Can construct a triangle from two sides and the included angle
Can explain why placing the angle elsewhere can yield two different triangles

question.prompt: Given sides of 5 cm and 7 cm and an angle of 40°, when is the constructed triangle guaranteed to be unique?

options.text: When the 40° angle is placed BETWEEN the 5 cm and 7 cm sides
Wherever the angle is placed — two sides and an angle always fix the triangle
Only when the angle is placed opposite the 7 cm side
options.diagnosis: A non-included angle is exactly the ambiguous SSA case — the arc can cross the ray twice.

options.text: Only if the angle is at least 60°
options.diagnosis: Invented threshold; uniqueness depends on the angle's POSITION, not its size.

question.explanation: With the angle included, the two sides and the opening between them leave exactly one way to finish — the SAS criterion. With a non-included angle, the closing arc can meet the ray in two places, producing two genuinely different triangles.

micros.title: Constructing a Triangle from ASA
micros.description: Draw the given side and copy the two given angles at its ends; when the data gives a NON-included side, first find the third angle via the 180° sum, justifying each step aloud.
outcomes: Can construct a triangle from two angles and the included side
Can convert AAS data to ASA using the angle-sum property

micros.title: Constructing a Right Triangle from RHS
micros.description: Erect a perpendicular at one end of a leg, then cut the hypotenuse arc from the other end — with a one-line justification for every arc, so the steps are reasons, not ritual.
outcomes: Can construct a right triangle given the hypotenuse and one side
Can justify each construction step and connect it to the RHS criterion

micros.title: Perimeter or Area? Choosing the Right Measure
micros.description: Re-anchor the two measures with actions — WALK the boundary (perimeter) vs COVER the surface (area) — and sort mixed word problems into P-questions and A-questions before solving any.
outcomes: Can decide whether a context calls for perimeter or area
Can compute both for rectangles and squares as revision

question.prompt: A rectangular plot is 20 m by 30 m. How much fencing is needed to enclose it?

options.diagnosis: Added one length and one breadth but forgot the other two sides.
Doubled only the 30 m sides, ignoring the two 20 m sides.

question.explanation: Fencing runs along the BOUNDARY, so it is a perimeter question: 2 × (20 + 30) = 100 m. The number 600 is 20 × 30 — the AREA in square metres, which measures the surface inside, not the fence around it.

micros.title: Area of a Parallelogram: Base × Perpendicular Height
micros.description: Slice the slanted end off a paper parallelogram and slide it across to make a rectangle — area = base × height, where the height is the measurement carrying the right-angle mark, never the slant side.
outcomes: Can compute a parallelogram's area choosing the correct base–height pair
Can reject a slant side offered as a 'height'

question.prompt: A parallelogram has base 10 cm, slant side 6 cm, and perpendicular height 4 cm on that base. What is its area?

options.diagnosis: Multiplied the slant side by the height — neither a valid base–height pair.

question.explanation: Area = base × perpendicular height = 10 × 4 = 40 cm². The 6 cm slant side is a distractor: the height must meet the base at 90°. Halving to 20 borrows the triangle's ½, which the parallelogram formula does not have.

micros.title: Area of a Triangle: Half a Parallelogram
micros.description: Cut a parallelogram along a diagonal into two identical triangles — so triangle area = ½ × base × perpendicular height, with the ½ earned, not memorised.
outcomes: Can compute triangle areas with the correct base–height pair
Can explain where the ½ comes from

question.prompt: Find the area of a triangle with base 12 cm and height 5 cm.

options.diagnosis: Added base and height instead of multiplying.
Halved the SUM of base and height — the ½ applies to the product.

question.explanation: Area = ½ × 12 × 5 = 30 cm². Without the ½ you get 60 — the area of the parallelogram that TWO copies of this triangle would tile, which is exactly why the half is there.

micros.title: Circumference of a Circle
micros.description: Wrap a string around a tin — about 3 diameters and a bit — to meet π, then use C = 2πr (or πd) with π ≈ 22/7 or 3.14 for wheels, tracks and trundle problems.
outcomes: Can compute circumference from radius or diameter
Can solve rotation-distance problems (how far one wheel turn travels)

question.prompt: Taking π = 22/7, find the circumference of a circle with radius 14 cm.

options.diagnosis: Computed πr, forgetting the factor 2 — only half the boundary.
Computed 2r (the diameter) and never multiplied by π.

question.explanation: C = 2πr = 2 × (22/7) × 14 = 88 cm. The value 616 is πr² — the AREA formula applied by mistake. Dimension check: circumference is a length, so r appears once, never squared.

micros.title: Area of a Circle
micros.description: Cut a circle into thin sectors and rearrange them into a near-rectangle of width r and length πr — so area = πr², with careful radius-vs-diameter reading in every problem.
outcomes: Can compute a circle's area from its radius or diameter
Can keep 2πr and πr² apart using dimension sense

question.prompt: Taking π = 22/7, find the AREA of a circle whose DIAMETER is 14 cm.

options.diagnosis: Squared the diameter instead of the radius — using d in place of r quadruples the area.
Computed r² = 49 but forgot to multiply by π.

question.explanation: Radius = 14 ÷ 2 = 7 cm, so area = πr² = (22/7) × 49 = 154 cm². Using 14 directly gives 616 — four times too big. And 44 is the circumference 2πr, a LENGTH answering a different question.

micros.title: Paths, Borders and Combined Figures
micros.description: Find areas of paths around or across parks by subtracting rectangles, handle figures built from rectangles, triangles and semicircles, and convert between cm² and m² where needed.
outcomes: Can compute the area of a uniform path around or through a rectangle
Can decompose a combined figure into standard shapes and convert area units

micros.title: Collecting and Organising Data
micros.description: Move from raw lists to frequency tables with tally marks, and pose the chapter's driving question: what ONE number could speak for this whole data set?
outcomes: Can build a frequency table from raw data
Can read simple summaries (largest, smallest, most common) from the table

micros.title: The Mean as Equal Sharing
micros.description: Level cube towers to see the mean as the equal-share value — total ÷ count — which may be a decimal and need not appear anywhere in the data.
outcomes: Can compute the mean of a data set
Can explain why the mean can be a value not in the list

question.prompt: Find the mean of 1, 4, 6 and 9.

options.diagnosis: Found the total but forgot to divide by the number of values.
Divided the total 20 by 5 — miscounted the number of values.

question.explanation: Mean = (1 + 4 + 6 + 9) ÷ 4 = 20 ÷ 4 = 5. Note that 5 is not one of the data values — perfectly fine. Picking 6 'because the mean should be in the list' forces the answer into the data, which the mean never promises.

micros.title: The Median: Sort First, Then Find the Middle
micros.description: Line the data up in order — a non-negotiable first step — then take the middle value (or the mean of the middle two) as the median.
outcomes: Can find the median of odd- and even-sized data sets after sorting
Can show how skipping the sort produces a wrong median

question.prompt: Find the median of 11, 2, 9, 4, 7.

options.diagnosis: Computed the mean (33 ÷ 5) instead of the median.

question.explanation: Sort first: 2, 4, 7, 9, 11. With five values the middle (third) is 7. Taking the middle of the UNSORTED list gives 9 — sorting is precisely what makes the median a genuine 'middle of the data'.

micros.title: Mode and Range
micros.description: MOde = MOst often — the most frequent value, found easily from a frequency table — and range = largest minus smallest, a first measure of spread.
outcomes: Can find the mode(s) and range of a data set
Can keep mode, maximum and mean verbally and computationally distinct

micros.title: Which Average Represents the Data Best?
micros.description: Pit the three averages against each other on skewed data — one luxury flat among modest rents — and choose the representative that honestly answers the question asked.
outcomes: Can choose an appropriate average for a context and justify the choice
Can explain how an outlier drags the mean but not the median

micros.title: Bar Graphs and Double Bar Graphs
micros.description: Choose a sensible scale, draw bar graphs, and use DOUBLE bars to compare two data sets side by side — this year's marks against last year's.
outcomes: Can draw a bar graph with an appropriate scale
Can read and compare paired categories from a double bar graph

micros.title: First Steps in Probability
micros.description: Assign probabilities as favourable outcomes over total EQUALLY LIKELY outcomes, placing events on the 0-to-1 scale — and testing by experiment that 'it happens or it doesn't' is not 50-50.
outcomes: Can list equally likely outcomes and compute simple probabilities
Can place impossible, unlikely, even, likely and certain events on the 0–1 scale

question.prompt: A fair die is rolled once. What is the probability of getting a number greater than 4?

options.diagnosis: Compared favourable with UNfavourable outcomes (2 against 4) — part-to-part odds, not probability.
Counted only the 6, forgetting that 5 is also greater than 4.

question.explanation: The favourable outcomes are 5 and 6 — two of six equally likely faces — so P = 2/6 = 1/3. 'Greater than 4 or not' are two DESCRIPTIONS, not two equally likely outcomes, so the 50-50 instinct fails.
